Concepts: the model in one page

Source: vignettes/concepts.Rmd
concepts.Rmd

This page gives the intuition behind every function in the package, with no code. Each section ends with a pointer to the article that shows it in practice.

The question

You measured the same features (genomic positions, days, proteins…) in two or more experimental groups, with several replicates per group. You want to know, feature by feature or as a whole, how different the groups are, with an honest account of the uncertainty that few replicates leave.

Data: one row per observation

Every analysis starts from a long table with five columns: ID (the feature), Group, Sample (the replicate), Input (a numeric position for the feature) and Output (the measurement). Input is what gives the features a geometry: two features with close Input values are expected to behave alike. See Basic pipeline and Real data.

The kernel: encoding “close features behave alike”

A kernel is a function k(x, x') returning how strongly two features at positions x and x' co-vary. A Squared Exponential kernel says the correlation decays smoothly with distance, at a rate set by its length scale; adding a noise term accounts for measurement noise, and a variance term sets the overall amplitude. These few numbers are the hyperparameters, and they are learned from the data by maximum likelihood (fit_kernel()), not chosen by hand. See Kernel choice.

The posterior: what we believe about each group

With the kernel fixed, each group gets a posterior distribution over its vector of feature values: a mean (the smoothed, replicate-averaged profile) and a covariance (how uncertain each feature is, and how uncertainties are tied together). Fewer replicates give a wider posterior; a shared kernel means groups are described by the same notion of closeness. posterior_mean() computes this in closed form. See Pooled vs. non-pooled and Unequal sample sizes.

Comparing groups: a distance between posteriors

Comparing two groups means comparing two Gaussian posteriors. Two summaries cover most needs:

  • the overlapping coefficient (OVL): the share of probability mass the two posteriors have in common, from 0 (disjoint) to 1 (identical);
  • the Wasserstein distance, a distance in the units of the data, which we normalise per feature so that it does not grow with the number of features.

OVL is intuitive but saturates near 0 once many features are compared jointly; the normalised Wasserstein stays readable. group_diff() picks between them for you from the number of features. See Choosing a metric and More than two groups.

Scale: when there are many features

The posterior involves a covariance matrix as large as the number of features, and inverting it becomes costly. Block-diagonal fitting splits the features into independent blocks, trading a little cross-block correlation for a much smaller problem per block. See Block-diagonal partition and Performance at a glance.

Assumptions to keep in mind

  • Within a group, each feature sits at one Input position (or one position per dimension), and every group being compared shares the same set of features.
  • Replicates of a feature within a group are exchangeable: the model has no built-in notion of pairing or batch.
  • Posteriors are Gaussian: the model targets continuous, roughly symmetric measurements (transform counts or proportions first when needed).

Glossary

Term Meaning
ID Identifier of a feature (position, protein, day…)
Input Numeric location of a feature; drives the kernel
Input_ID Index of the dimension when Input has several
Kernel Function giving the covariance of two features from their positions
Hyperparameters Kernel parameters (variance, length scale, noise) fitted from the data
Posterior Distribution of a group’s feature vector given the data
pooled TRUE: one kernel for all groups; FALSE: one per group
OVL Overlapping coefficient between two posteriors, in [0, 1]
Wasserstein Distance between two posteriors, in the data’s units
Block Subset of features fitted independently of the others
